Gideon v. Wainwright. In 1963, the Supreme Court established that the Sixth Amendment guarantees the right to counsel in all criminal trials, and, crucially, that the government must provide an attorney to defendants who cannot afford one.

Clarence Earl Gideon was arrested in Florida for breaking and entering in a poolroom, a felony punishable by up to five years. He asked the trial judge for a public defender because he had no money. The judge refused, citing Florida law, which provided counsel only in capital cases. Gideon was forced to conduct his own defense. Unable to navigate procedure, challenge evidence, or present a coherent case, he was convicted and sentenced to five years.

From prison, Gideon filed a handwritten petition for a writ of certiorari. The Supreme Court recognized the constitutional importance and granted it. The question was urgent: Does the Sixth Amendment guarantee a right to counsel, and if so, must the state provide one for indigent defendants? A 1942 case called Betts v. Brady had held that the right to counsel was not automatic but depended on circumstances—age, education, complexity. Most states did not appoint counsel in non-capital felonies.

Justice Black wrote for a unanimous Court. The Sixth Amendment states that in all criminal prosecutions, the accused shall have the assistance of counsel for his defense. The right to counsel is fundamental to a fair trial. A defendant without a lawyer is at a severe disadvantage. From the very beginning, state and national constitutions and statutes have laid great emphasis on procedural safeguards designed to protect the accused. The necessity of a lawyer's help has been universally recognized. The Court overruled Betts v. Brady. Counsel is a right in all criminal prosecutions, not dependent on case-by-case circumstances. States must provide attorneys for indigent defendants in felony cases, and this applies to states through the Fourteenth Amendment.

Gideon held that counsel is a constitutional right but did not specify how states must provide it. States established public defender offices and appointed counsel systems. The quality and funding have been a perennial problem. Argersinger v. Hamlin extended Gideon to misdemeanor cases where the defendant was imprisoned. Scott v. Illinois later limited it: counsel is required only if the defendant actually receives a prison sentence, not if the case could result in imprisonment. Courts have addressed whether Gideon guarantees effective assistance of counsel, and the answer is yes.

Public defender systems are chronically underfunded. Public defenders often carry enormous caseloads and lack resources for investigation. The right to counsel is formally guaranteed but practically compromised in many jurisdictions. Death penalty cases, where stakes are highest, typically receive better counsel than routine felonies, an irony Gideon did not foresee. Yet Gideon himself was vindicated. On retrial with counsel, he was acquitted. The case exemplifies how a single Supreme Court decision can reshape an entire system and establish a constitutional bedrock for fairness.
